articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than construction. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 3 of 27 planned drainage projects
Public records show $8.4 million spent on engineering consultants and administrative costs while construction spending totaled $6.1 million
County officials blame permitting delays and inflation, but internal emails reveal repeated scope changes and contractor disputes
articles.body:
The intersection of Ninth Avenue and Fairfield Drive floods every time it rains more than two inches. It flooded last Tuesday. It flooded three weeks before that. It has flooded, by one resident's count, forty-seven times since Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee in November 2023.

That fee was supposed to fix this. Voters were told it would.

"We will finally have the resources to address our drainage infrastructure in a systematic, comprehensive way," County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said at the time. The county projected $15 million annually for construction. Fairfield Drive sat near the top of the priority list.

Three years later, the project hasn't broken ground. Neither have twenty-three others on that original list.

Following the Money

Public records obtained by The Flightline through a series of requests over four months paint a picture of a program that has struggled to translate revenue into results.

Since the fee took effect in January 2024, Escambia County has collected $47.2 million from property owners. The fee appears on tax bills as a separate line item—$84 annually for a typical single-family home, more for commercial properties based on impervious surface area.

Of that $47.2 million, the county has spent $6.1 million on actual construction. Three projects have been completed: a culvert replacement in Bellview, a retention pond expansion near the airport, and ditch improvements along Highway 29 north of Cantonment.

Engineering consultants have received $8.4 million.

Administrative costs—including three new full-time positions in the Public Works department, vehicles, software, and office expenses—account for another $4.7 million.

The remaining $28 million sits in a dedicated fund, earning interest but not fixing drainage.

The Consultant Question

Volkert Inc., a Mobile-based engineering firm, holds the county's primary stormwater consulting contract. The firm has billed $5.2 million since 2024 for design work, environmental assessments, and project management services.

That figure surprised even some county staff. An internal email from March 2025, written by a Public Works project manager whose name was redacted, flagged the spending to department leadership.

"We are approaching design costs that exceed what we budgeted for construction on several projects," the email states. "I want to make sure we have justification documented before the next audit."

The response, from Public Works Director Derek Hess, noted that scope changes and additional environmental reviews had increased costs but were "necessary to ensure projects are permitted correctly the first time."

Volkert did not respond to requests for comment.

Permitting and Delays

County officials point to regulatory hurdles as a primary cause of delays. Many stormwater projects require permits from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, the Army Corps of Engineers, or both. Wetland impacts trigger additional review.

"We inherited a system that was neglected for decades," Hess said in an interview. "When you try to fix it, you're dealing with environmental constraints that didn't exist when these neighborhoods were built."

The Fairfield Drive project illustrates the challenge. Initial plans called for widening drainage swales and adding a retention area on adjacent county-owned land. But a 2024 environmental survey found jurisdictional wetlands on the parcel. The county now needs a wetland mitigation plan, which Hess said could add eighteen months to the timeline.

"We can't just bulldoze wetlands," he said. "There's a process."

Residents who have attended commission meetings to complain about flooding have heard variations of this explanation for three years. Some are skeptical.

"They knew about those wetlands before they put the project on the list," said Marcus Webb, who has lived on Fairfield Drive for twenty-two years. "They used it to sell us on the fee. Now it's the excuse for why nothing happens."

Scope Creep and Contractor Disputes

Internal documents reveal other obstacles that haven't been discussed publicly.

A drainage improvement project in the Brownsville neighborhood was designed in 2024 and bid out in early 2025. The low bidder, a Pensacola contractor, was rejected after county staff determined the company lacked experience with the required pipe diameter. The second-lowest bidder's price came in $1.8 million over the engineer's estimate.

Rather than award the contract, the county sent the project back to Volkert for redesign. Records show $340,000 in additional design fees. The project rebid this spring. Construction is now scheduled for fall 2027.

On at least four other projects, county commissioners requested changes after designs were completed—adding features, extending boundaries, or incorporating adjacent problems that weren't in the original scope. Each change required new engineering work and, in some cases, new environmental review.

"The commission has a hard time saying no to constituents," said one county employee who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss internal matters. "Every time someone shows up with flooding pictures, there's pressure to add their street to whatever project is closest. That's how a $2 million job becomes a $5 million job that never gets built."

What Happens Now

The County Commission is scheduled to receive a stormwater program update at its July 10 meeting. Staff will recommend prioritizing five projects for construction in the next fiscal year, using accumulated fund balances.

Commissioner Bergosh, who championed the original fee, said he remains confident the program will deliver.

"Rome wasn't built in a day," he said. "We're building capacity. We're doing the engineering right. These projects will get built."

He acknowledged that spending to date hasn't matched public expectations.

"Could we have communicated better about the timeline? Probably. But the money is there. It's not going anywhere else. And when these projects are done, they'll work."

The commission has not discussed reducing the fee or altering its structure. Current projections show the fund balance growing to $45 million by the end of fiscal year 2027, assuming construction spending remains at current levels.

Meanwhile, the National Weather Service forecasts a 70 percent chance of above-normal rainfall for the Gulf Coast this summer.

At Ninth and Fairfield, Marcus Webb has started parking his truck on higher ground when storms approach. He bought a sump pump last year. He watches the drainage ditch behind his house fill up every time the sky darkens.

"They've got my money," he said. "I'd like to see some pipe in the ground."

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Fish House on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Joe Patti's wholesale operation has survived four hurricanes and two decades of condo development. This summer, the family faces a choice.
brief: The Patti family's wholesale fish operation on Pensacola Beach is one of the last working waterfronts on the island, surrounded by condominiums and resort developments.
A Miami-based developer has offered $4.2 million for the property, which sits on 1.3 acres of waterfront land near the Pensacola Beach Boardwalk.
Frank Patti Jr., 67, says the family will decide by August whether to sell or invest in repairs needed after damage from Hurricane seasons past.
articles.body:
The ice machine kicks on at 4:15 a.m., same as it has for thirty-two years. Frank Patti Jr. doesn't need an alarm. He's been waking to that sound since he was thirty-five years old, back when his father still ran the morning shift and the beach had more bait shops than bars.

Now Frank is sixty-seven. His father has been dead for nine years. And the fish house—a low-slung concrete block building with a rusted metal roof and the words "PATTI SEAFOOD WHOLESALE" barely visible in faded red paint—sits like a relic between a fourteen-story condominium and a parking garage that charges eighteen dollars a day.

"We used to be the nice building on this stretch," Frank said, standing in the sorting room where mullet and sheepshead lay packed in ice. "Now we're the eyesore."

The Patti family fish house is the last commercial fishing operation on Pensacola Beach. It occupies 1.3 acres of waterfront property on the Santa Rosa Island Authority leasehold, a plot that a Miami-based developer has valued at $4.2 million. The offer came in March. Frank has until August to give an answer.

Four hurricanes and counting

The building has survived Ivan in 2004, Dennis in 2005, Sally in 2020 and Idalia in 2023. Each storm left its mark. The west wall still shows a waterline from Ivan's surge. A steel I-beam, installed after Dennis, runs across the ceiling of the main processing room. The walk-in freezer dates to 1987 and runs on a compressor that Frank describes as "held together by duct tape and stubbornness."

The most recent damage came from Idalia, which sideswiped the Panhandle as a Category 3 before making landfall in the Big Bend. Storm surge flooded the sorting room with three feet of water. The forklift was a total loss. Insurance covered $47,000 of an estimated $130,000 in damage.

"Every hurricane, you rebuild a little less," Frank said. "At some point you have to ask what you're rebuilding for."

A family business in transition

Joe Patti Sr. started the wholesale operation in 1994, three years after selling his share of the famous Joe Patti's Seafood retail market on Main Street. The beach location was supposed to be smaller, simpler—a way to stay in the business without the retail headaches. He ran it until a stroke in 2014 forced him to hand the keys to Frank.

Frank's son, Joey, is thirty-four. He works as a marine surveyor in Mobile and comes down on weekends when he can. He has two young daughters. He has not committed to taking over the business.

"I told him I wouldn't guilt him into it," Frank said. "This life isn't for everybody. It's early mornings and fish guts and never taking a vacation during red snapper season. If his heart's not in it, the business dies anyway. Just slower."

Joey Patti declined to be interviewed for this article.

The developer's pitch

The offer comes from Coastal Vista Partners, a Miami-based firm that has developed mixed-use properties in Destin, Panama City Beach and Orange Beach over the past decade. According to documents filed with the Santa Rosa Island Authority, the company envisions a "boutique waterfront hotel" with 120 rooms, ground-floor retail and a rooftop restaurant.

The $4.2 million offer is for the Patti family's leasehold interest and the building. The land itself belongs to SRIA, which leases beachfront property under a system established in 1947.

Marcus Webb, a Coastal Vista vice president, said the company approached the Pattis after noticing the property during a site survey last fall.

"We see an opportunity to activate an underutilized waterfront parcel," Webb said in a phone interview. "The location is exceptional. We'd bring jobs, tax revenue and a property that complements the beach's identity."

Webb said the company has made no formal application to SRIA pending the Patti family's decision.

What the neighbors think

Opinion on the beach is divided, though not evenly.

At the Sandbar, a restaurant two blocks east, owner Diane Kutsch said she'd hate to see the fish house go.

"Frank's the real deal," she said. "Half the restaurants on this beach buy from him. You lose that, you're buying frozen fish from Sysco like everybody else."

But at a condominium owners association meeting last month, several residents of the adjacent Gulf Tower complained about truck traffic, the smell of fish waste and what one speaker called "an aesthetic incompatible with the investment we've made in our properties."

SRIA board member Tammy Bohannon said the authority has received no formal complaints about the Patti operation.

"They're a legacy business," Bohannon said. "They've been good tenants. Whatever happens next, that's the family's decision to make."

A question without an easy answer

On a Tuesday morning last week, Frank Patti stood at the dock behind the fish house, watching a shrimp boat unload its catch. Pelicans circled. The sun was already brutal at 7 a.m. He wore rubber boots, a faded Crimson Tide cap and a t-shirt that said "Patti Seafood" in lettering so cracked it was nearly illegible.

Four million dollars is more money than his father ever made in the business. It would mean retirement. Travel. Time with his grandchildren. No more 4 a.m. wake-ups. No more insurance claims. No more wondering if the next hurricane would be the one that finished the job.

"My dad built this," Frank said. "Not the building. The relationships. Thirty years of fishermen trusting us to buy their catch. Thirty years of restaurants trusting us to sell them something fresh. You can't put a price on that."

He paused.

"But they did put a price on it. And I'd be lying if I said I wasn't thinking about it."

The shrimp boat pulled away from the dock. Frank walked back inside to sort the catch. The ice machine hummed. The sun climbed higher over the condominiums, throwing the fish house into shadow.

articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors and a Reckoning for Beach Road
articles.dek: With the July show days away, Pensacola Beach residents are asking why the same traffic plan keeps failing.
brief: An estimated 200,000 visitors will descend on Pensacola Beach for the July 10-11 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show
Residents and business owners say the existing traffic management plan has failed for three consecutive years
Santa Rosa Island Authority officials acknowledge problems but say infrastructure limits their options
articles.body:
The line starts forming on Pensacola Beach Boulevard before sunrise. By 7 a.m. on air show Saturday, it will stretch past the toll plaza, past the Bob Sikes Bridge, past the Tiger Point intersection where drivers sit with their engines idling and their patience thinning.

This is the annual ritual of Blue Angels Homecoming weekend. And for residents of Pensacola Beach, it has become something else: a referendum on whether anyone in charge is paying attention.

"We've been saying the same thing for years," said Martha Kellerman, who has lived on Via de Luna Drive since 2011. "The traffic plan doesn't work. Everyone knows it doesn't work. And every July they roll out the same plan."

The 2026 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show is scheduled for July 10-11, with practice sessions on July 8-9. Event organizers expect approximately 200,000 visitors across the two show days, according to figures provided by the Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce. That estimate tracks with attendance numbers from recent years.

The Santa Rosa Island Authority, which governs the beach, released its traffic management plan last week. It mirrors previous years: temporary no-parking zones along Pensacola Beach Boulevard, shuttle buses from the Pensacola Bay Center, and Escambia County Sheriff's Office deputies stationed at key intersections.

A familiar gridlock

During the 2025 show, traffic backups on the Bob Sikes Bridge exceeded three hours on Saturday afternoon. Some drivers abandoned their vehicles and walked. Emergency responders reported delayed response times to minor incidents on the island.

Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons acknowledged the problem at a county commission meeting in August 2025. "We had too many cars trying to get to the same place at the same time," he said. "That's a math problem we haven't solved."

The math has only gotten more difficult. Pensacola Beach's year-round population has grown by an estimated 15 percent since 2020, according to U.S. Census estimates. Short-term rental properties have proliferated. The number of hotel rooms on the island has increased by 340 since 2018.

Yet the infrastructure remains unchanged. The Bob Sikes Bridge, completed in 1960 and reconstructed in 1990, remains the only vehicular access point to the island. Pensacola Beach Boulevard is still two lanes in each direction.

'We're not building another bridge'

At a Santa Rosa Island Authority board meeting on June 18, several residents urged the authority to consider more aggressive measures: mandatory shuttle service, parking reservations, or capping the number of vehicles allowed on the island.

Board Chairman Thomas Campanella said the authority had studied such options. "The reality is, we're not building another bridge," he said. "We're not widening the road. We have to work with what we have."

What they have, critics say, is a plan designed for a smaller crowd in a different era. The shuttle system, which runs from the Pensacola Bay Center parking garage, transported approximately 4,200 passengers on air show Saturday in 2025. That represents roughly 4 percent of total attendance.

"The shuttles are great if you know about them and you're willing to use them," said Jim Reeves, owner of Flounder's Chowder House on Pensacola Beach. "Most people don't know and aren't willing."

Reeves said the traffic situation cuts both ways for beach businesses. The air show brings massive crowds—and massive revenue—but it also traps his staff in gridlock and frustrates customers who can't find parking.

What other cities do

Other coastal communities hosting major events have experimented with stricter traffic controls. Fort Lauderdale implemented a reservation system for beach parking during spring break in 2024. Panama City Beach uses a tiered pricing structure that increases parking fees during peak events.

Pensacola Beach has resisted such measures. The Santa Rosa Island Authority generates significant revenue from parking fees during the air show—$847,000 during the 2025 event, according to authority records. A reservation system could potentially reduce that figure.

Campanella said the board would revisit traffic management after this year's show. "We're open to new ideas," he said. "But any changes would need to be studied carefully."

For Kellerman, the Via de Luna resident, that response sounds familiar. She has attended four authority meetings since 2022 to raise concerns about air show traffic. Each time, she said, officials promised to study the issue.

"Studying is what you do when you don't want to do anything," she said. "Meanwhile, the rest of us sit in traffic."

The Blue Angels will take to the sky in two weeks. The cars will line up before dawn. And on Pensacola Beach, the argument about what to do next will continue—at least until next July.
